rulings.name: Domanic v. Christian Brothers Automotive Corporation
rulings.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
rulings.summary: The court affirmed summary judgment for a Christian franchisor on a Jewish applicant’s § 1981 claim.  It distinguished religious discrimination from ancestry-based discrimination and found no evidence that the Christian-only franchise policy masked racial discrimination.  The majority did not decide the asserted ministerial-exception defense.

rulings.name: Young v. Mississippi Valley State University
rulings.court: U.S. District Court, Northern District of Mississippi
rulings.summary: A graduate student alleged that her university restricted religious content in her academic work.  The court dismissed her claims against the university without prejudice because Eleventh Amendment immunity barred the suit.  It did not resolve the merits of the alleged First Amendment violation.

rulings.name: In re Cindy Clemishire and Jerry Lee Clemishire
rulings.summary: The Texas Supreme Court granted temporary stay relief while considering a mandamus challenge to two church-autonomy decisions involving Gateway Church and the Morris defendants.  The order did not decide the merits of the ecclesiastical-abstention question.
rulings.statusNote: Stay issued September 18.  Later docket status has not been independently confirmed.

rulings.name: Doe, as next friend of C.F. v. McDonald
rulings.summary: The Court denied an application for an injunction pending appeal in a challenge concerning a religious exemption from school vaccination requirements.  Justices Alito and Gorsuch would have granted the application.  The unexplained order did not resolve the merits of the religious-liberty challenge.
rulings.statusNote: Emergency relief denied; no merits opinion.

rulings.name: Young v. NHE Inc.
rulings.court: U.S. District Court, Northern District of Mississippi
rulings.summary: The court dismissed a former employee’s religious-discrimination and religious-speech claims.  The Title VII claim was untimely, and the complaint did not allege facts making the private employer a governmental actor subject to First Amendment restrictions.  The dismissal rested on those legal barriers rather than a trial determination of the discrimination allegations.

rulings.name: In re Institute in Basic Life Principles, Inc.
rulings.court: Texas Sixth Court of Appeals, Texarkana
rulings.summary: The court conditionally granted mandamus directing the trial court to vacate an overbroad discovery order in a civil abuse-related lawsuit.  It resolved the dispute under procedural discovery rules rather than deciding IBLP’s constitutional objection.  It also instructed further proceedings to respect earlier guidance against inquiries into protected religious doctrine.
rulings.statusNote: The constitutional question was not decided.  This was not a blanket religious privilege or immunity from suit.
matchNames: In Re Institute in Basic Life Principles, Inc. v. the State of Texas

rulings.name: In re Gateway Church, Willbanks, Fambro, and Minor
rulings.court: Texas Fifth Court of Appeals, Dallas
rulings.summary: The court held that defamation-related claims against Gateway Church and three elders were inseparable from the church’s investigation and communications concerning its pastor.  It conditionally directed dismissal under ecclesiastical abstention.  The opinion expressly did not decide whether the challenged statement was defamatory.
rulings.statusNote: Later development: the Texas Supreme Court issued a stay on September 18, 2026.  Later docket status has not been independently confirmed.

rulings.name: Anyanwu v. City of San Antonio (CPS Energy)
rulings.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
rulings.summary: The court affirmed summary judgment on a former employee’s federal and Texas discrimination claims, including religion.  Disagreement with an independent workplace investigation did not create a genuine factual dispute that the stated reason for termination was a pretext for discrimination.
rulings.statusNote: The opinion is not designated for publication.  It addresses proof of discrimination, rather than a religious-accommodation claim.
matchNames: Anyanwu v. City of San Antonio

rulings.name: Greater New Hamilton Grove Baptist Church v. Hamilton Grove Missionary Baptist Church
rulings.summary: A church and trustee argued that ecclesiastical abstention barred judicial intervention in a disputed cemetery burial.  The Court of Appeals dismissed their appeal as moot because the challenged injunction had already been dissolved and the underlying matter dismissed without prejudice.  It did not decide whether ecclesiastical abstention applied.
matchNames: Greater New Hamilton Grove Baptist Church and Tommie Burns v. Hamilton Grove Missionary Baptist Church

rulings.name: Jeremiah Counsel Corporation v. Young
rulings.summary: In a dispute over Second Baptist Church of Houston’s governance, the court barred claims requiring it to evaluate religious descriptions or second-guess ecclesiastical decisions.  It separately applied neutral corporate-law principles, invalidating a 2023 amendment to the church’s articles while rejecting the challenge to its bylaws.  The mixed ruling illustrates the boundary between protected church autonomy and enforceable secular corporate requirements.
rulings.statusNote: An accounting claim remained; the order did not dismiss the entire lawsuit.

rulings.name: Sri Shirdi Sai Baba Temple of Austin v. Lam
rulings.summary: The court held that neutral Texas corporate law could resolve a temple’s governance dispute without deciding religious questions.  Its certificate of formation controlled over conflicting bylaws that purported to shift management from directors to members.  The court granted defendants’ summary-judgment motion and denied plaintiffs’ motion, while leaving attorney’s fees for later determination.
rulings.statusNote: Attorney’s fees remained pending; this was not a final judgment.

rulings.name: Young v. Town of Coffeeville
rulings.court: U.S. District Court, Northern District of Mississippi
rulings.summary: The court rejected an unpaid municipal intern’s claims arising from restrictions on unsolicited religious discussions with town-hall visitors.  It found insufficient evidence of municipal liability or an underlying First Amendment violation and credited the town’s interest in efficient public services.  Any Title VII theory had been abandoned and also failed because the internship was unpaid.

rulings.name: Davis v. Guerrero
rulings.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
rulings.summary: The court affirmed denial of habeas relief to a Texas death-row prisoner who challenged the use of his Satanist affiliation and materials at sentencing.  Applying AEDPA’s deferential standard, it held that the state court’s rejection of his First Amendment claim did not conflict unreasonably with clearly established Supreme Court law.
rulings.statusNote: This is a deferential federal habeas decision, not a general authorization to punish religious belief.

rulings.name: East Plano Islamic Center v. Texas Funeral Services Commission
rulings.court: U.S. District Court, Western District of Texas
rulings.summary: The court allowed EPIC’s individual-capacity claims against former commission presiding officer Kristin Tips to proceed.  It held that allegations of religiously discriminatory enforcement against Islamic funeral rites sufficiently pleaded violations of clearly established Free Exercise and Equal Protection rights.  This denied Tips’s motion to dismiss; it was not a final finding that all allegations were proved.
rulings.statusNote: This order addressed Tips’s motion.  It reserved the commission defendants’ separate motion.

rulings.name: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety
rulings.summary: The Court affirmed dismissal of a Rastafarian prisoner’s RLUIPA damages claims against Louisiana corrections officers who allegedly forcibly shaved his head.  Because the officers had not knowingly and voluntarily agreed to personal liability under the statute’s federal-funding conditions, the Spending Clause did not permit those claims.  The Court did not decide whether RLUIPA otherwise authorizes money damages.
matchNames: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections
Landor v. Louisiana Dept. of Corrections and Public Safety
Landor v. Louisiana Dept of Corrections and Public Safety Revisions: 6/24/26

rulings.name: Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe
rulings.summary: Falun Gong practitioners alleged that Cisco supplied surveillance technology enabling religious persecution in China.  The Court reversed and remanded, holding that federal courts cannot create new causes of action under the Alien Tort Statute for violations of international norms and that the Torture Victim Protection Act does not authorize aiding-and-abetting liability.
rulings.statusNote: A civil-remedies decision involving religious-persecution allegations, rather than a domestic Free Exercise holding.

rulings.name: Leach v. Gateway Church
rulings.court: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Texas
rulings.summary: The court dismissed congregants’ claims challenging Gateway Church’s allocation of donated tithes.  Applying Fifth Circuit church-autonomy precedent, it concluded that deciding whether spending fulfilled the church’s religious mission would require an impermissible inquiry into ecclesiastical matters.  The ruling closed the civil action; it did not adjudicate whether the alleged financial misconduct occurred.

rulings.name: The Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod v. Christian
rulings.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
rulings.summary: The court revived the denomination’s suit concerning Concordia University Texas’s separation from church governance.  It held that the jurisdictional dismissal improperly substituted a secular interpretation of the church’s religious structure and remanded for further proceedings.  The decision did not finally resolve control or ownership.
